title: Ordering Genes with Double Mutants
endLine: Combine opposite mutants in a pathway: the later gene usually wins.

scenes.tts: Two genes steer one cell fate, but which acts first? In hermaphrodite Caenorhabditis elegans, development makes one thousand ninety somatic cells. The same one hundred thirty-one die every time, leaving nine hundred fifty-nine. Reproducible death alone does not prove genes cause it, so geneticists test mutants.
scenes.caption: Two genes steer one cell fate, but which acts first? In hermaphrodite Caenorhabditis elegans, development makes 1,090 somatic cells. The same 131 die every time, leaving 959. Reproducible death alone does not prove genes cause it, so geneticists test mutants.
scenes.visual: Establish the one carried world (schematic, filling most of the frame height): a transparent worm outline holding a glowing horizontal cell-fate track from a pulsing cell on the left, past two unmarked question-mark gates, to a fate readout on the right (Lives vs Dies). Slow flow pulses drift continuously left to right. Before the numbers are spoken, a clean counter ticks 1,090 cells, highlights 131 routing to Dies, and settles on 959 living cells; then the question-mark gates brighten as the narrator turns to mutants.
scenes.narration: Two genes steer one cell fate, but which acts first? In hermaphrodite Caenorhabditis elegans, development makes 1,090 somatic cells. The same 131 die every time, leaving 959. Reproducible death alone does not prove genes cause it, so geneticists test mutants.

scenes.visual: The carried schematic cell-fate track dims slightly while pulses keep drifting smoothly behind full-opacity title text: Ordering Genes with Double Mutants.

scenes.tts: Start with loss-of-function mutants, where a gene's activity is reduced or abolished. A null mutant has none left. Losing ced nine removes a brake on death, so killing follows. Losing ced three removes the killer, so doomed cells live. Single mutants name the parts, not their order.
scenes.caption: Start with loss-of-function mutants, where a gene's activity is reduced or abolished. A null mutant has none left. Losing ced-9 removes a brake on death, so killing follows. Losing ced-3 removes the killer, so doomed cells live. Single mutants name the parts, not their order.
scenes.visual: On the same carried schematic track, two gates settle before being named: a brake gate (ced-9) and a killer gate (ced-3). First, the ced-9 gate cracks open and drops away; flow surges along the track and the cell routes to Dies. The track resets; next, the ced-3 gate cracks open and drops away; flow halts and the doomed cell routes to Lives. Both single-mutant outcomes sit side by side as the two gates swap positions with a question mark to show order is still unknown.
scenes.narration: Start with loss-of-function mutants, where a gene's activity is reduced or abolished. A null mutant has none left. Losing ced-9 removes a brake on death, so killing follows. Losing ced-3 removes the killer, so doomed cells live. Single mutants name the parts, not their order.

scenes.tts: To order them, geneticists put both mutations into one worm, making a double mutant. Suppose ced nine sits upstream as a brake holding back ced three. In that order, ced three acts downstream, carrying out the death that ced nine normally prevents.
scenes.caption: To order them, geneticists put both mutations into one worm, making a double mutant. Suppose ced-9 sits upstream as a brake holding back ced-3. In that order, ced-3 acts downstream, carrying out the death that ced-9 normally prevents.
scenes.visual: Still on the carried schematic track, the two single-mutant views merge into one worm outline holding both gates in line: ced-9 (Brake) upstream on the left, with a flat blocking bar reaching forward to hold back ced-3 (Killer) downstream on the right, which points to Dies. Gentle pulses queue behind ced-9, visually showing that ced-9 stops death only by restraining ced-3.
scenes.narration: To order them, geneticists put both mutations into one worm, making a double mutant. Suppose ced-9 sits upstream as a brake holding back ced-3. In that order, ced-3 acts downstream, carrying out the death that ced-9 normally prevents.

scenes.tts: Now remove both genes in the same worm, breaking the brake and the killer together. Predict what happens to the cells in this double mutant. Do they die because the brake is gone, or live because the killer is gone too?
scenes.caption: Now remove both genes in the same worm, breaking the brake and the killer together. Predict what happens to the cells in this double mutant. Do they die because the brake is gone, or live because the killer is gone too?
scenes.visual: On the carried schematic track, both the ced-9 brake gate and the ced-3 killer gate crack open and drop away together. Flow pulses rush past the empty brake slot, reach the empty killer slot, and stall at a bright question mark between Lives and Dies. A full-opacity question card appears cleanly above the track: Die without the brake, or live without the killer?
scenes.narration: Now remove both genes in the same worm, breaking the brake and the killer together. Predict what happens to the cells in this double mutant. Do they die because the brake is gone, or live because the killer is gone too?

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause on the carried schematic track: both broken gate slots and the question card remain steady on screen while the question mark between Lives and Dies gently pulses.

scenes.tts: The double mutant lives and keeps the cells that normally die, matching the ced three mutant. Removing the killer cancels the effect of removing the brake, so the brake works through the killer. That is epistasis: when two losses have opposite effects, the double mutant usually shows the later gene's effect.
scenes.caption: The double mutant lives and keeps the cells that normally die, matching the ced-3 mutant. Removing the killer cancels the effect of removing the brake, so the brake works through the killer. That is epistasis: when two losses have opposite effects, the double mutant usually shows the later gene's effect.
scenes.visual: The question card clears; the stalled pulses at the missing ced-3 slot fade out and the cell routes smoothly to Lives, glowing with the same colour as the ced-3 single mutant. A clean directional arrow locks in from ced-9 (upstream) to ced-3 (downstream), with a full-opacity banner below the schematic track: Epistasis: later gene wins.
scenes.narration: The double mutant lives and keeps the cells that normally die, matching the ced-3 mutant. Removing the killer cancels the effect of removing the brake, so the brake works through the killer. That is epistasis: when two losses have opposite effects, the double mutant usually shows the later gene's effect.

scenes.tts: Two limits keep epistasis honest. First, the rule expects a linear pathway and opposite loss-of-function mutations. Experimenters use strong loss-of-function or null mutants, because leftover activity can blur which phenotype wins. Comparing the double mutant to both single mutants tests which phenotype truly wins.

scenes.visual: On the carried schematic track, the linear chain highlights alongside two opposite-outcome badges (Dies vs Lives). Each gate shows a clean empty null slot (activity abolished; no leftover activity) rather than a leaky half-open gate, and two compact reference markers for the single mutants align beside the double-mutant readout so the winning phenotype can be checked directly.
scenes.narration: Two limits keep epistasis honest. First, the rule expects a linear pathway and opposite loss-of-function mutations. Experimenters use strong loss-of-function or null mutants, because leftover activity can blur which phenotype wins. Comparing the double mutant to both single mutants tests which phenotype truly wins.

scenes.tts: Second, genetic order does not show which proteins touch. The textbook cartoon draws ced nine holding ced four, a partner that switches on ced three. The phenotypes stand, yet the mechanism stays less settled. A 2024 study tested ced nine mutants that cannot bind ced four. They still protected cells in those assays.
scenes.caption: Second, genetic order does not show which proteins touch. The textbook cartoon draws CED-9 holding CED-4, a partner that switches on CED-3. The phenotypes stand, yet the mechanism stays less settled. A 2024 study tested CED-9 mutants that cannot bind CED-4. They still protected cells in those assays.
scenes.visual: Zoom smoothly onto the carried schematic track between the CED-9 gate and an intermediate CED-4 gate (no molecular structures, simple geometric blocks). A dashed clasp connecting CED-9 and CED-4 appears, then dissolves while the genetic-order arrow beneath stays solid. A label appears (2024 assays): the non-binding CED-9 block separates physically from CED-4, yet the cell readout on the right stays safely on Lives.
scenes.narration: Second, genetic order does not show which proteins touch. The textbook cartoon draws CED-9 holding CED-4, a partner that switches on CED-3. The phenotypes stand, yet the mechanism stays less settled. A 2024 study tested CED-9 mutants that cannot bind CED-4. They still protected cells in those assays.

scenes.tts: Within those limits, epistasis unlocked landmark pathways. In 1986, Hilary Ellis and Horvitz reported two cell-death genes, ced three and ced four. Robert Horvitz's laboratory combined mutations to order four genes. E G L one blocks ced nine, and ced nine holds back ced four. In turn, ced four switches on ced three.
scenes.caption: Within those limits, epistasis unlocked landmark pathways. In 1986, Hilary Ellis and Horvitz reported two cell-death genes, ced-3 and ced-4. Robert Horvitz's laboratory combined mutations to order four genes. EGL-1 blocks CED-9, and CED-9 holds back CED-4. In turn, CED-4 switches on CED-3.
scenes.visual: Pull back on the carried schematic worm track as it expands cleanly to four modular gates in order from left to right: EGL-1, CED-9, CED-4, CED-3 (labelled schematic, at most six elements). First CED-3 and CED-4 illuminate (1986), then EGL-1 and CED-9 slot in upstream. Moving left to right as spoken, EGL-1 drops a blocking bar onto CED-9, releasing CED-9's hold on CED-4, which sends a bright activation pulse to CED-3 and routes the cell to Dies.
scenes.narration: Within those limits, epistasis unlocked landmark pathways. In 1986, Hilary Ellis and Horvitz reported two cell-death genes, ced-3 and ced-4. Robert Horvitz's laboratory combined mutations to order four genes. EGL-1 blocks CED-9, and CED-9 holds back CED-4. In turn, CED-4 switches on CED-3.

scenes.tts: Double mutants also ordered yeast secretion. In 1980, Novick, Field and Schekman found one hundred eighty-eight clones that trapped the enzyme invertase at thirty-seven degrees Celsius. They sorted them into twenty-three groups. Their sec numbers carried no order, so 1981 double mutants ordered those handoffs. Combine two mutations in one pathway, and the winning outcome maps their order.
scenes.caption: Double mutants also ordered yeast secretion. In 1980, Novick, Field and Schekman found 188 clones that trapped the enzyme invertase at 37 °C. They sorted them into 23 groups. Their SEC numbers carried no order, so 1981 double mutants ordered those handoffs. Combine two mutations in one pathway, and the winning outcome maps their order.
scenes.visual: The carried schematic pathway track smoothly transforms from the worm outline into a yeast cell outline keeping the same left-to-right handoff grammar (schematic, no molecular structures). Cargo dots (invertase) pile up at 37 °C behind scrambled numbered SEC gates (188 clones, 23 groups, 1980); then double-mutant pairing clicks those gates into an ordered left-to-right secretion sequence (1981), letting the pathway direction glow cleanly from start to finish.
scenes.narration: Double mutants also ordered yeast secretion. In 1980, Novick, Field and Schekman found 188 clones that trapped the enzyme invertase at 37 °C. They sorted them into 23 groups. scenes.visual: The schematic track gently fades behind a high-contrast dark end card showing only the core rule in full-opacity text: 'Combine opposite mutants in a pathway: the later gene usually wins.'
